KEYWORDS: bicycle removal, bike disposal, donate bike, recycle bike, junk removal  

# Bicycle Removal and Disposal: Every Option  

**The quickest answer:** you can get rid of a bike for free by donating, recycling, or selling it, and you only pay a junk‑removal service like 1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK when you need labor, a large volume, or a same‑day pickup.  

Below is a step‑by‑step guide that ranks every realistic option from cheapest to most expensive, explains how each works, and shows real pricing so you can pick the best route for your situation.

---

## 1. Assess Your Bike Situation  

Before you start hunting for a solution, know exactly what you have.

### 1.1 Quantity and Size  
| Item | Approx. Volume (ft³) | Typical Weight |
|------|----------------------|----------------|
| Standard road/ mountain bike | 2‑3 | 25‑35 lb |
| Folding bike (collapsed) | 1‑1.5 | 20‑30 lb |
| E‑bike (battery included) | 3‑4 | 45‑70 lb |
| Tandem or cargo bike | 4‑5 | 50‑80 lb |

### 1.2 Condition  
- **Rideable** – can be sold or donated.  
- **Repairable** – consider fixing and then selling/donating.  
- **Beyond repair** – look at recycling or scrap metal options.

### 1.3 Location & Access  
If the bike is on a balcony, in a garage, or behind a locked gate, you’ll need a service that offers **on‑site loading** (e.g., 1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK). If it’s already on the curb, curbside pickup may be free.

---

## 2. Free & Low‑Cost Options  

### 2.1 Donate to Charity or Thrift Stores  

- **Goodwill, Salvation Army, local bike co‑ops** accept gently used bikes.  
- Most will pick up a single bike for free if you call ahead; some require you to drop it off.  
- **Tip:** Clean the bike, remove personal items, and take off the front wheel to fit a standard car trunk.

### 2.2 Recycle Through Municipal Programs  

Many cities run **bike‑recycling days** or accept bikes at curbside bulk‑pickup depots.  

- **How to schedule:** Visit your city’s waste‑management website, fill out a bulk‑pickup request, and select “bike” as the item.  
- **Cost:** Usually **free** for residents; some locales charge a nominal **$5‑$10** tipping fee.  
- **What’s accepted:** Whole bikes, broken frames, and even e‑bike batteries (some cities require separate battery drop‑off).

### 2.3 Sell or Give Away Online  

- **Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, OfferUp** – post photos, describe condition, set a price (often $30‑$150 for a decent bike).  
- **Free giveaway:** List as “Free” and you’ll likely get a neighbor or student to haul it away.  

### 2.4 Scrap Metal Yards  

If the bike is rusted beyond repair, you can **sell the metal**.  

- **Typical price:** $0.10‑$0.20 per pound of steel/aluminum.  
- **Example:** A 30‑lb steel bike yields **$3‑$6**.  
- **Process:** Call the yard, ask about accepted items, and bring the bike on a trailer or in a pickup truck.  

**Why these are usually best:** No hidden fees, you may even earn a little cash, and you keep the bike out of landfill.

---

## 3. DIY Disposal Methods  

### 3.1 Curbside Bulk Pickup  

- **Eligibility:** Most U.S. municipalities allow up to 1‑2 bikes per household per bulk‑pickup request.  
- **Steps:**  
  1. Log in to your city’s waste portal.  
  2. Schedule a pickup date (usually 1‑2 weeks out).  
  3. Place the bike at the curb, wheel‑first, with the front wheel removed if needed.  
- **Fees:** Often **$0**, but some cities charge a **$10‑$15** bulk‑pickup surcharge.  

### 3.2 Drop‑Off at Recycling Centers  

- **Find a center:** Use Earth911 or your local landfill’s website.  
- **What to bring:** Bike, any detachable battery (e‑bike), and a photo ID for hazardous‑waste logs.  
- **Cost:** Typically **free**, though some centers levy a **$5‑$10** tipping fee for metal.  

### 3.3 Disassemble for Easier Transport  

- **Tools needed:** Allen keys, screwdriver, wrench.  
- **Procedure:** Remove wheels, pedals, chain, and seat post. Pack parts in a sturdy box or bike bag.  
- **Benefit:** Fits in a car trunk, eliminating the need for a truck or trailer.  

---

## 4. Paid Junk‑Removal Services  

When you have **multiple bikes, heavy e‑bikes, limited time, or no vehicle**, a junk‑removal service becomes a practical fallback.

### 4.1 1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK? – What You Pay For  

- **Pricing model:** Volume‑based, measured in 1/8‑truck increments.  
- **Minimum load (1/8 truck)** – **$100‑$150** (truck space: 1.25 ft L × 5 ft H × 8 ft W).  
- **Small loads:** **$107‑$396**.  
- **Medium loads:** **$396‑$600**.  
- **Large loads:** **$600‑$1,099**.  
- **Average job:** **≈ $240** across all customers.  
- **Single‑item removals:** **$70‑$400** depending on bulk/weight (a single bike usually falls in the lower end of this range).  

**What’s included:**  
- All labor and loading from anywhere on your property (no curb‑side move needed).  
- Hauling, disposal, and recycling fees.  
- Post‑removal cleanup.  
- Licensed and insured crew.  

**How to book:**  
- Online form or call **1‑800‑468‑5865**.  
- No price quote online or over the phone; you get a **free on‑site estimate** (no credit card required).  
- Crew calls **25‑30 minutes** before arrival.  
- Same‑day service often available.  

**Flex product:** If you can load the bike yourself into a bag or container, Flex starts at **$39** (you handle loading, they collect).  

### 4.2 Competitor Pricing Snapshot  

| Company | Minimum Charge | Volume‑Based Range* | Per‑Item Pricing | Notes |
|---------|----------------|--------------------|------------------|-------|
| **1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK?** | $100‑$150 (1/8‑truck) | $107‑$1,099 (small‑large) | $70‑$400 per bike | On‑site estimate, all‑inclusive |
| **LoadUp** | $89 minimum | N/A (price per item) | Fixed per‑item price (varies by item) | Guaranteed online price, 20‑30% cheaper on average |
| **Junk King** | $99 minimum | $389‑$488 (half‑truck) • $589‑$658 (full‑truck) | N/A | Approximate online estimate, confirmed on site |
| **College Hunks Hauling Junk** | $150‑$750 per job | Volume‑based | N/A | $99 dispatch fee added after booking |

\*Ranges reflect typical volume‑based pricing; actual cost varies by market (high‑cost metros hit the upper end, Midwest/South hit the lower end).  

### 4.3 When Paid Service Is the Right Choice  

- **You have 3+ e‑bikes** (heavy batteries make DIY loading tough).  
- **No vehicle** and the bike is on a high floor or locked garage.  
- **Time‑critical** (moving day, rental turnover).  
- **You prefer “all‑in‑one”**: crew loads, hauls, disposes, and cleans up.  

### 4.4 Worked Dollar Example  

**Scenario:** You need to remove 4 standard bikes (≈ 30 lb each) and 1 heavy e‑bike (≈ 70 lb). You live in a suburb where a half‑truck load is the smallest volume the crew will send.

1. **Volume needed:** 4 bikes + 1 e‑bike ≈ 5 ft L × 5 ft H × 8 ft W → roughly a **half‑truck** (5 ft L).  
2. **1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK? half‑truck price:** **$400‑$600** (mid‑range for most metros).  
3. **Add possible battery fee (if in CA, CT, RI):** $10.50 per e‑bike battery.  
4. **Total estimate:** **$410‑$610**.  

**Compare with LoadUp:**  
- Assume LoadUp charges **$120 per bike** (average online price).  
- 5 bikes × $120 = **$600** (no extra battery fee).  

**Result:** In a mid‑cost metro, **1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK? could be $190‑$190 cheaper** than LoadUp, especially when the crew handles the heavy e‑bike battery safely.

---

## 5. Special Cases: Larger Two‑Wheel Vehicles & Related Items  

### 5.1 Motorcycles & Scooters  

- **Title transfer & DMV** – You must surrender the title, remove plates, and notify the DMV.  
- **Salvage yards** – Accept whole motorcycles for scrap; value is **$0.10‑$0.20 per lb** of metal.  
- **Donation** – Some charities accept working motorcycles; they may arrange pickup.  

### 5.2 RVs and Travel Trailers  

- **Why harder than a car:** Fiberglass bodies, built‑in propane tanks, and large appliances (refrigerators, water heaters) require special handling.  
- **Disposal options:**  
  - **Sell/Donate** if functional – Craigslist or local RV clubs.  
  **- Scrap metal** – Weight‑based tipping fees (often $30‑$50 per ton).  
  - **Junk removal** – Most paid services treat RVs as **large‑item** pickups; expect a **full‑truck** price (**$600‑$1,099** with 1‑800‑GOT‑JUNK?).  
- **Regulations:** Some states require de‑registration and removal of hazardous fluids before disposal.

### 5.3 Construction Debris (if you’re clearing a bike‑repair shop)  

- **Accepted by many landfills** but often incurs a **weight‑based tipping fee** (≈ $80‑$120 per ton).  
- **Recycling facilities** may take metal frames for scrap; check local metal‑recycling centers for fees.  

**Bottom line:** For anything larger than a standard bike, start with **title transfer**, then explore **sale/donation**, and only resort to **paid junk removal** if you lack transport or the item is heavily damaged.

---

## 6. Common Mistakes People Make  

| Mistake | Why It Costs You More | How to Avoid |
|---------|----------------------|--------------|
| **Assuming “free” curbside pickup includes e‑bike batteries** | Batteries are hazardous; many cities charge a separate fee or refuse them. | Call your waste agency first; if a fee applies, factor it in or remove the battery yourself. |
| **Leaving the bike on the curb without a ticket** | Some cities issue fines for “illegal dumping.” | Always schedule a pickup or obtain a bulk‑pickup ticket. |
| **Over‑estimating the value of scrap metal** | Steel fetches only $0.10‑$0.20 / lb, so a $200 bike yields <$6. | Treat scrap as a **last‑resort** option, not a profit source. |
| **Booking a junk‑removal service without confirming volume** | You may be quoted a full‑truck price for a half‑truck load, wasting $300‑$500. | Measure or estimate volume; ask for a **volume‑based** quote before confirming. |
| **Using expired coupon codes** | Leads to surprise “price higher than expected” at checkout. | Rely on **verified discounts**: email‑list offers ($10‑$25 off) or local franchise promotions. |
